lesson.title: Reading Expressions the Way Python Does
lesson.summary: Python evaluates a mixed expression using a strict, predictable order of operations, and misreading that order is one of the most common sources of silent logic bugs in conditional code.
lesson.body:
Every programming language needs a rulebook for what happens first when an expression mixes several kinds of operators in one line. You already know one version of this from math class: parentheses before exponents before multiplication and division before addition and subtraction. Python follows a similar idea but extends it to cover comparisons like < and ==, and to cover the logical operators and, or, and not. Without a fixed order, the expression x > 2 and x < 10 or x == 0 would be ambiguous, and different readers (or different runs of the program) might interpret it differently. Python removes that ambiguity by defining exactly which operator binds tightest.

For boolean expressions, the order that matters most is this: parentheses are evaluated first, then arithmetic (with ** highest, then unary plus and minus, then multiplication, division, floor division, and remainder, then addition and subtraction), then comparisons (<, >, <=, >=, ==, !=), and only after all of that does Python touch the logical operators. Among the logical operators themselves, not binds tightest, and binds next, and or binds loosest. This mirrors how the earlier building blocks fit together: operator precedence in general, and the logical operators and, or, and not specifically, combine into one consistent set of rules rather than a pile of special cases.

Trace a concrete example. Let x = 5, and evaluate x > 2 and x < 10 or x == 0. Python first resolves the comparisons, since they outrank the logical operators: x > 2 becomes True, x < 10 becomes True, and x == 0 becomes False. The expression is now True and True or False. Next Python applies and, which binds tighter than or, so True and True collapses to True. That leaves True or False, which evaluates to True. The final result is True, and if you only skimmed the expression without knowing the precedence order, you might have grouped the or with the second comparison first and reached a different, wrong conclusion.

Precedence also explains why not True and False and not (True and False) are different expressions with different answers. In the first, not binds only to the True immediately next to it, so it becomes (not True) and False, which is False and False, which is False. In the second, the parentheses force Python to evaluate True and False as a unit first, giving False, and then negate the whole thing, giving True. Same three words, same operators, opposite results, purely because parentheses override the default binding order.

The practical lesson is not to memorize the table and never use parentheses again. It is the opposite: once you know the default order, you know exactly where a reader might get confused, and you can add parentheses there even when Python does not require them. A condition like (age >= 13) and (has_permission or is_admin) is no more correct than the version without parentheses, but it is far easier for a human to check at a glance, and being able to make that judgment call is the real payoff of understanding order of operations.
